title: The Brighton Square House to the Zurichberg: Dublin, Trieste, Zurich, Paris, and the Book of One Day
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Rathgar House and the Fall

stops.name: 41 Brighton Square, Rathgar: the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested. The date is firm; the coordinate is not the one the atlas inherited. Two lenses gave two different wrong pins for this house, 53.3234,-6.2653 and 53.3183,-6.2664, both of them in Rathmines rather than Rathgar. OSM/Nominatim is followed here.
stops.campa: In a redbrick terrace house on a small square in Rathgar, on the second of February, a son is born to John Stanislaus Joyce, rate collector, and Mary Jane Murray. Three days later he is carried to St Joseph's in Terenure and baptized James Augustine. The father is a Cork man with a good tenor voice, a talent for company, and no talent whatever for money; ten children will follow and the family will move house more than a dozen times, each address a little further down. The square still stands. So does the plaque.
suggested_refs: The commemorative plaque at 41 Brighton Square, Rathgar
St Joseph's Church, Terenure, where the baptism was registered on 5 February 1882

stops.name: 1 Martello Terrace, Bray: the seafront years
stops.date_confidence: attested for the residence 1887-1891; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinate corrected from 53.2028,-6.0983, which is Bray town centre rather than the terrace.
stops.campa: The father is appointed a rate collector and the fortunes turn upward for four years. The family takes a seafront house on Martello Terrace, the Irish Sea at the door, and here at a Christmas table the argument over Parnell and the priests is fought out in front of a child who is old enough to listen. He will set it down almost unaltered thirty years later in the first chapter of A Portrait, the goose going cold, Dante leaving the room, the father weeping into his hands. Nothing in the scene is invented except the names.
suggested_refs: 1 Martello Terrace, Bray, Co. Wicklow, the house of the Portrait Christmas dinner

stops.name: Clongowes Wood College, Clane: the boarder of six
stops.date_confidence: attested for September 1888; day unknown, defaulted to 01. Coordinate corrected from 53.2839,-6.6934, roughly 3 km south of the college.
stops.campa: At six he is sent as a boarder to the Jesuits at Clongowes, the youngest boy in the school, small enough that the others ask him his name and his age as though he were a curiosity. He is pushed into a ditch of cold slimy water, catches fever, lies in the infirmary; he is pandied by the prefect of studies for broken glasses he did not break, and walks the length of the corridor to the rector to say so. Three years later the fees stop coming and he is taken away. He leaves with three years of Latin, and with the ditch, the corridor and the pandybat, which go into the first chapter of A Portrait without disguise.
suggested_refs: Clongowes Wood College archives, Clane, Co. Kildare
The castle corridor and rector's study of the Portrait pandying scene

stops.name: North Richmond Street, Dublin: the step down
stops.date_confidence: attested by Ellmann only, and present in the geography lens alone; the chronology lens omits the episode entirely. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: There is no money for fees. For a stretch of 1893 the boy is enrolled with the Christian Brothers on North Richmond Street, a charity school for the sons of clerks and dockers, and his father takes it as a public humiliation: a Jesuit-schooled son of his handed to the Brothers. Parnell is two years dead. The household is now moving northward across the river, address by address, each one smaller. He is eleven. North Richmond Street will open Araby twenty years later, blind at one end, with an empty two-storey house standing in a square of ground at the other.
suggested_refs: The Christian Brothers school, North Richmond Street, Dublin

segments.name: Belvedere, the Green, and the Reading Room

stops.name: Belvedere College, Great Denmark Street: the free place
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1893-1898; the month is not fixed in any source and is defaulted. Coordinate corrected from 53.3546,-6.2606, about 180 m off 6 Great Denmark Street.
stops.campa: Father John Conmee, who was rector at Clongowes and remembers the smallest boy in the school, arranges free places at Belvedere for Joyce and his brothers. He takes the national examination prizes and hands the prize money to his father, who spends it. He is offered the Jesuit novitiate and does not take it. Somewhere in these five years the retreat sermon on hell is preached at him, and somewhere on the strand at Dollymount a girl standing in the water looks back at him, and both go into the book whole.
stops.quote: Heavenly God! cried Stephen's soul, in an outburst of profane joy.
stops.quote_source: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, Chapter 4 (the bird-girl on the strand); verified verbatim against the Wikisource text
suggested_refs: Belvedere College, 6 Great Denmark Street, Dublin
The strand at Dollymount, setting of the Portrait epiphany

stops.name: Newman House, St Stephen's Green: the Ibsen review
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1900 publication in The Fortnightly Review; the month is defaulted. Ellmann's further claim that the review drew Ibsen's own attention is reconstruction, unverified here.
stops.campa: He reads English, French and Italian at University College Dublin, housed in two Georgian buildings on the south side of the Green. At eighteen he publishes a review of Ibsen's When We Dead Awaken in a London journal and is paid twelve guineas, the first money his writing earns. He learns Dano-Norwegian to read the plays untranslated. His classmates are being made into the professional Catholic middle class of a country that does not yet exist; he is teaching himself, in a language nobody around him wants, to leave.
suggested_refs: Newman House, 85-86 St Stephen's Green, then University College Dublin
'Ibsen's New Drama', The Fortnightly Review, 1 April 1900

stops.name: National Library of Ireland, Kildare Street: the Hamlet theory
stops.date_confidence: attested for repeated readership across 1898-1904; no single date exists and the year is placed at the midpoint, month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Under the domed reading room on Kildare Street he sits through the student years among the periodicals and the librarians. He will give the room to Stephen Dedalus and put in his mouth an argument that Shakespeare is not the prince but the ghost, the dead father speaking to a son named for a dead son, and let the Dublin literary men in their chairs half listen and disbelieve. From Trieste and Zurich he will write home for the Dublin street directories he can no longer walk in and consult, and check the tram routes of 1904 by post.
stops.quote: A man of genius makes no mistakes. His errors are volitional and are the portals of discovery.
stops.quote_source: Ulysses, episode 9 (Scylla and Charybdis), the library scene; standard attribution, not verified against the episode text in this pass
suggested_refs: The domed reading room of the National Library of Ireland, Kildare Street
Ulysses, episode 9, set in this building

stops.name: Hotel Corneille, rue Corneille: the medical student who does not study medicine
stops.date_confidence: attested for December 1902 to April 1903; the day of arrival is not fixed and is defaulted.
stops.campa: He graduates from the Royal University in October, enrolls at the Catholic University Medical School, and within weeks is gone to Paris to study medicine there instead. He does not study medicine there either. He lodges near the Odeon, reads at the Bibliotheque Sainte-Genevieve, writes epiphanies on scraps, and lives on money his family cannot spare, sent by a father who has nothing. In January he abandons the studies altogether. He is twenty, he owes money in two cities, and he writes home for more.
stops.quote: I want to achieve myself, little or great as I may be, for I know that there is no heresy or no philosophy which is so abhorrent to my church as a human being, and accordingly I am going to Paris.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Lady Augusta Gregory, November 1902; the doubled negative is the corrected reading, confirmed across six independent editions via Open Library full-text search. Some editions read 'the church' for 'my church'.
suggested_refs: The Hotel Corneille, rue Corneille, Paris, lodging of the first exile
The Bibliotheque Sainte-Genevieve reading room

stops.name: Glasnevin Cemetery, Dublin: the mother buried
stops.date_confidence: attested for the death, 13 August 1903; the burial at Glasnevin followed on 17 August, and the stop is dated to the death.
stops.campa: A telegram brings him back from Paris: mother dying come home father. Mary Jane Joyce dies of cancer in August, forty-four years old, having borne fifteen children and buried five. At the bedside his uncle John Murray gestures angrily for the family to kneel and pray. James and Stanislaus stay standing. The refusal is not staged and no one applauds it; it costs him the household, and he gives it to Stephen Dedalus in the first chapter of Ulysses, where Buck Mulligan raises it before breakfast.
stops.quote: I will not serve that in which I no longer believe, whether it call itself my home, my fatherland, or my church.
stops.quote_source: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, Chapter 5 (Stephen to Cranly); widely quoted, not verified against the chapter text in this pass
suggested_refs: The grave of Mary Jane Joyce, Glasnevin Cemetery, Dublin

stops.name: Finn's Hotel, Leinster Street South: Nora Barnacle
stops.date_confidence: attested. Coordinate corrected from 53.3417,-6.2503, which lands on Lincoln Place about 230 m east of the hotel.
stops.campa: He stops a tall young woman on Nassau Street, red-haired, from Galway, a chambermaid at Finn's Hotel around the corner. She takes him for a Swede on the strength of his eyes. They arrange to meet and she does not come; they arrange again. On the sixteenth of June they walk out together to Ringsend, and he will set the whole of Ulysses on that one day, eighteen years later and in another country. She has read almost nothing he will ever write. She stays thirty-seven years.
suggested_refs: Finn's Hotel, 1-2 Leinster Street South, Dublin, where Nora Barnacle worked
Ringsend, destination of the walk of 16 June 1904

stops.name: Martello Tower, Sandycove: the week with Gogarty
stops.date_confidence: attested for September 1904; the exact days are not fixed and the sources disagree on the length, six nights against about a week. The date given is approximate within the month. Coordinate corrected from 53.2903,-6.1131, which contradicted the atlas's own afterlife pin by 190 m.
stops.campa: Oliver St John Gogarty, medical student and wit, rents a Napoleonic gun tower on the point at Sandycove and takes Joyce in as a guest. It lasts about a week. In the night the other lodger, Samuel Chenevix Trench, dreams of a black panther and fires a revolver; Gogarty takes the gun and fires it again, at the pans over Joyce's bed. Joyce dresses and walks into Dublin in the dark. Eighteen years later the tower opens his novel, stately and plump, and Gogarty spends the rest of his life being Buck Mulligan.
suggested_refs: The Martello tower at Sandycove Point, opening setting of Ulysses

segments.name: The Berlitz Road: Zurich, Pola, Trieste

stops.name: Zurich Hauptbahnhof: the post that does not exist
stops.date_confidence: attested for October 1904; the day of arrival is not fixed in the reachable sources and is approximate within the month.
stops.campa: In October he and Nora leave Ireland together, unmarried, through London and Paris, on the strength of a Berlitz teaching post an agency has promised him in Zurich. They arrive and the post does not exist. They stay about a week while the agency redirects him to Trieste, where there is also no post, and from Trieste he is sent on again to Pola at the far end of the Adriatic. The exile begins as a clerical error and lasts thirty-six years. He will die in this city.
stops.quote: All things are inconstant except the faith in the soul, which changes all things and fills their inconstancy with light.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Lady Augusta Gregory, November 1902; widely cited, not verified against a letters edition in this pass
suggested_refs: Zurich Hauptbahnhof, arrival point of both Joyce's Zurich exiles

stops.name: Berlitz School, Via Giulia, Pola: English for the naval officers
stops.date_confidence: attested for the residence October 1904 to March 1905; the day is approximate within the month of arrival.
stops.campa: At the southern tip of Istria, in the chief naval port of Austria-Hungary, he teaches English to officers of the imperial fleet and lodges with a fellow teacher, Alessandro Francini Bruni. He calls the place a naval Siberia in his letters home and asks Stanislaus for books. Nora is pregnant and speaks no Italian. He is drafting the stories that will be Dubliners in a town he despises, about a city he has left, in a language the officers around him are paying to acquire.
suggested_refs: The Berlitz School, Via Giulia, Pola (Pula), Austria-Hungary
The letters of James Joyce from Pola, 1904-1905

stops.name: Berlitz School, Via San Nicolo, Trieste: the transfer
stops.date_confidence: attested for March 1905; the day is defaulted. Coordinate corrected from 45.6494,13.7724, about 180 m off the street.
stops.campa: A spy scare runs through Pola and the authorities expel the foreigners. Joyce, twenty-three, is transferred to the Berlitz branch in Trieste, the imperial port where Italian, Slovene, German and Greek are spoken in the same street and nobody is quite a native. It suits him exactly. He will live here eleven years, longer than in any other city of his life. Dubliners, A Portrait and the first episodes of Ulysses are written here, at this distance from the streets they name.
suggested_refs: The Berlitz School branch, Via San Nicolo, Trieste

stops.name: Via Giovanni Boccaccio, Trieste: Giorgio born
stops.date_confidence: attested for the birth date; the address is reconstruction, and the geography lens states plainly that biographers dispute which room this was.
stops.campa: A son is born in a rented room in July and they name him Giorgio. Which room is not certain; the biographers place the family at three addresses in that year and agree on none. In June Joyce has printed a satirical broadside, The Holy Office, against the Dublin literary men he left behind; no printer and no place of issue are recorded for it. In October Stanislaus arrives from Dublin to teach at the same school and is at once absorbed into paying for a household he did not make. He will do it for a decade, and be thanked for it rarely.
suggested_refs: The disputed Trieste lodging of July 1905, birthplace of Giorgio Joyce

segments.name: Rome, the Return, and the Eleven Years

stops.name: Via Frattina 52, Rome: the bank clerk
stops.date_confidence: attested for the arrival, 31 July 1906. The chronology lens dated the move to May 1906, which is the month the Berlitz director absconded with the school's funds, not the month of the move.
stops.campa: The Berlitz director in Trieste absconds with the funds in May and Joyce takes a post as correspondence clerk at the bank of Nast, Kolb and Schumacher on Via S. Claudio. He, Nora and the baby arrive on the last day of July and lodge on Via Frattina. He writes eight and nine hours a day at another man's ledgers, hates the city with a completeness he reserves for very few things, is robbed of his month's wages in the street, and leaves after seven months. He takes one thing away with him: the idea for a story called The Dead.
suggested_refs: Via Frattina 52, Rome, the Joyce lodging of 1906-1907
The bank of Nast, Kolb & Schumacher, Via S. Claudio 87, Rome

stops.name: London: Elkin Mathews and Chamber Music
stops.date_confidence: attested for May 1907; the day is defaulted. The chronology lens dated this edition to 1906, which is wrong by a year.
stops.campa: Elkin Mathews brings out thirty-six short lyrics in London under the title Chamber Music, chosen by Stanislaus, arranged by Stanislaus, and published while the author is sitting in a Roman bank. They are Elizabethan in manner, delicate, and entirely unlike everything that follows. Joyce is twenty-five and has published a book. It sells poorly. He will later say the poems belong to a young man and that he was never a poet, and go on letting them be reprinted for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: Chamber Music (London: Elkin Mathews, May 1907), Joyce's first book

stops.name: Trieste: the fever, Lucia, and The Dead
stops.date_confidence: attested for Lucia's birth, 26 July 1907. This is the atlas's canonical Trieste pin, inherited byte-identical from freud.journey.json, dannunzio.journey.json and arnold_rikli.journey.json.
stops.campa: Back in Trieste in March on part-time work, he is struck in May by rheumatic fever and spends weeks in the public hospital, the family too poor that year to pay for anything better than a public ward. Nora is delivered of a daughter, Lucia, in the paupers' ward alongside him. Convalescing, he finishes The Dead, the last and longest story in Dubliners, seven years after he began the book. He will stay in this city, on and off, for eleven years, longer than anywhere else in his life.
stops.quote: His soul swooned slowly as he heard the snow falling faintly through the universe and faintly falling, like the descent of their last end, upon all the living and the dead.
stops.quote_source: Dubliners, closing sentence of 'The Dead'; verified verbatim against the Wikisource text
suggested_refs: The Ospedale Maggiore of Trieste, where Lucia Joyce was born
The canonical Trieste pin shared with Freud, d'Annunzio and Rikli

stops.name: Trieste city centre: the lessons to Italo Svevo
stops.date_confidence: attested for a friendship running roughly 1907-1913; no start date is recorded and the year is placed at the opening of the period, month and day defaulted. The onward claim that Svevo's protagonist shaped Leopold Bloom is a literary-historical inference, not a documented statement by Joyce.
stops.campa: A businessman in the marine paint trade takes English lessons for his Trieste office and turns out to have published two novels nobody read. Joyce reads them, tells Ettore Schmitz he has written literature, and quotes passages back to him from memory. Schmitz, who writes as Italo Svevo, begins again on the strength of it and produces La coscienza di Zeno at sixty-two. Meanwhile Joyce is turning the abandoned Stephen Hero into A Portrait, cutting a thousand pages down to five chapters.
stops.quote: For myself, I always write about Dublin, because if I can get to the heart of Dublin I can get to the heart of all the cities of the world.
stops.quote_source: Quoted in Richard Ellmann, James Joyce (rev. ed. 1983); secondary attribution only
suggested_refs: The Svevo-Joyce correspondence
Italo Svevo, La coscienza di Zeno (1923)

segments.name: Dublin Twice More, and the End of Ireland

stops.name: Bowling Green, Galway: the Barnacle house
stops.date_confidence: attested for the visits of 1909 and 1912; the month within 1909 is approximate and the day is defaulted. Coordinate corrected from 53.2724,-9.0508, about 290 m east.
stops.campa: He goes to Galway with Nora to meet the mother and the aunt who raised her, in a small house on Bowling Green behind the church. Annie Barnacle receives the Dublin man politely. Nora had a boy in Galway once, Michael Bodkin, who came to her window in the rain when he was ill and died soon after, and Joyce has already used him, and will use him again, and gives him at last to Gretta Conroy in a hotel room in Dublin with the snow beginning outside.
suggested_refs: The Nora Barnacle house, 8 Bowling Green, Galway
The grave of Michael Bodkin, Rahoon cemetery, Galway

stops.name: Volta Cinematograph, 45 Mary Street: Ireland's first cinema
stops.date_confidence: attested for the opening, 20 December 1909. The chronology lens dated the venture to October 1909, which is when Joyce arrived to set it up, not when the cinema opened.
stops.campa: He persuades four Triestine businessmen that Dublin has no cinema and could have one. He returns in October, finds premises on Mary Street, and opens the Volta two days before Christmas with an Italian programme that a city expecting something else does not much want. The backers withdraw within months and sell it at a loss. In January he goes back to Trieste with his sister Eileen. From this same Dublin autumn come the letters to Nora that no editor would print for sixty years.
stops.quote: I think I would know Nora's fart anywhere.
stops.quote_source: Selected Letters of James Joyce, ed. Richard Ellmann, from the 1909 letters to Nora Barnacle; not verified against the primary edition in this pass
suggested_refs: The Volta Cinematograph, 45 Mary Street, Dublin, opened 20 December 1909

stops.name: Maunsel and Company, Middle Abbey Street: the sheets burned
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1912; the month is approximate and the day is defaulted.
stops.campa: He comes back to Dublin a last time to force the publication of Dubliners, seven years after he first submitted it. George Roberts of Maunsel, afraid of libel over the real pubs and the real names and the mention of Edward VII, has the printed sheets destroyed rather than issue them. Joyce leaves the country with proofs he stole from the printer and writes a broadside in the voice of the man who burned them, Gas from a Burner, and posts it back to Dublin. He never sets foot in Ireland again.
suggested_refs: The Maunsel & Company offices, Middle Abbey Street, Dublin
'Gas from a Burner' (1912), printed in Trieste

stops.name: Via Donato Bramante, Trieste: the last prewar flat
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The geography lens states that this address sequence for 1912-1915 is pieced together from the letters; the year is placed at the midpoint and month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: In the last Trieste flat, above the city on the slope, Ezra Pound writes to him out of London in 1913 and becomes the engine of his career: the serialization, the patrons, the reviews. Joyce begins drafting Ulysses while A Portrait is still appearing in instalments. Buenos Aires, in the same decade, is reading Emin Arslan, who styles himself the Argentine authority on everything east of Trieste. Trieste is still Austrian and has five years left of being Austrian. Joyce sits above it, laying out Dublin street by street.
stops.quote: I want to give a picture of Dublin so complete that if the city suddenly disappeared from the earth it could be reconstructed out of my book.
stops.quote_source: Reported remark, quoted in Frank Budgen, James Joyce and the Making of Ulysses (1934); not verified against Budgen's text
suggested_refs: The Joyce flats of Via Donato Bramante and Via Scussa, Trieste, 1912-1915

stops.name: London: Grant Richards publishes Dubliners
stops.date_confidence: attested.
stops.campa: Eight and a half years after the manuscript first reached him, Grant Richards publishes Dubliners in London. Fifteen stories, no plot to speak of, a city rendered with the flatness of a police report and the last three pages of The Dead. It sells 379 copies in the first year, 120 of them bought by the author. The same year A Portrait begins in The Egoist and Joyce, thirty-two, opens the notebooks for a novel that will take place on the sixteenth of June 1904.
suggested_refs: Dubliners (London: Grant Richards, 15 June 1914)
The Egoist, serialization of A Portrait from February 1914

stops.name: Feldkirch station: out of Austria-Hungary on parole
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Ellmann alone gives the crossing and the date, with no document cited in the reachable material.
stops.campa: Italy declares war on Austria-Hungary in May and Trieste becomes a front. Joyce is a British subject in an enemy empire; he gives his parole not to take up arms and is allowed out with his family through the mountain frontier at Feldkirch, into neutral Switzerland. Stanislaus, who has been open about his irredentism, is interned instead. The brother who has paid for everything for ten years is not released until 1919, and the frontier closes between them.
suggested_refs: The Feldkirch frontier crossing, Vorarlberg, June 1915

stops.name: Universitatstrasse 38, Zurich: most of Ulysses
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Zurich residence 1915-1919; the specific date of taking this address is not fixed and is defaulted within the month of arrival.
stops.campa: For four years he lives on other people's money: the Royal Literary Fund, the British civil list, gifts from Edith Rockefeller McCormick, and then the standing subvention of Harriet Shaw Weaver, who will support him for the rest of his life and whom he meets rarely. In borrowed rooms in a city full of people waiting out a war, he writes most of Ulysses, episode by episode, posting each to London and New York as it is finished. Lenin is a few streets off on the Spiegelgasse, waiting for a train to Petrograd. Neither man knows the other is there.
stops.quote: Writing in English is the most ingenious torture ever devised for sins committed in previous lives.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Fanny Guillermet, 5 September 1918; not verified against a letters edition in this pass
suggested_refs: Universitatstrasse 38, Zurich
The Harriet Shaw Weaver subvention, from 1917

stops.name: Cabaret Voltaire, Spiegelgasse 1: the Dada adjacency
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Cabaret Voltaire's date, inherited byte-identical from laban.journey.json. The overlap with Joyce is city-level only: his own Zurich addresses appear nowhere in the atlas corpus, and no meeting is recorded.
stops.campa: A few streets from where Joyce is assembling Ulysses, Hugo Ball reads sound poems in a back room off the Niederdorf. Rudolf Laban's dance school runs through the same years in rooms lent by the Kunsthaus, and Laban's dancers cross the street to perform here: Suzanne Perrottet, Mary Wigman, Sophie Taeuber. In 1919 the twelve-year-old Vera Skoronel enters the school while Dada is still shouting. Nobody records the novelist and the dancers in the same room. The war put them in the same square mile.
stops.quote: History, Stephen said, is a nightmare from which I am trying to awake.
stops.quote_source: Ulysses, episode 2 (Nestor); verified verbatim against the Project Gutenberg text of the 1922 edition
suggested_refs: Cabaret Voltaire, Spiegelgasse 1, Zurich, opened 30 March 1916
The Laban school in the borrowed Kunsthaus rooms, Zurich 1915-1919

stops.name: Pension Daheim, Locarno: after the iridectomy
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Locarno stay, October 1917 to January 1918, at the Pension Daheim from 5 November. The geography lens called this the first of many eye crises, which is wrong: the iritis dated from Trieste around 1907.
stops.campa: In August, in Zurich, Ernst Sidler cuts an iridectomy into his right eye. He goes south to Locarno for the mild lake air and stays until January, in a pension on the Swiss side of a border that has Italy at war on the other. The eyes have been failing since Trieste and will go on failing: iritis, glaucoma, cataract, some dozen operations over twenty years, patches, leeches, cocaine, and long stretches when he can write only in crayon on cardboard in letters two inches high. Hermann Hesse is in the same small country, being analyzed by the Zurich school, waiting out the same war.
suggested_refs: The Pension Daheim, Locarno
Ernst Sidler's iridectomy on Joyce's right eye, Zurich, 24 August 1917

stops.name: Zurich: the English Players and Henry Carr
stops.date_confidence: attested for the first production, The Importance of Being Earnest, 29 April 1918. The venue is contradicted between sources: the geography lens says the Theater am Pfauen, the correction says the Theater zu den Kaufleuten, and no Pfauen link could be corroborated. Pinned to the canonical Zurich coordinate rather than adjudicate.
stops.campa: With the actor Claud Sykes he founds a company called the English Players to stage Wilde and Shaw and Synge in wartime Zurich. He recruits into the first cast an employee of the British Consulate named Henry Carr, quarrels with him over the takings and the price of a pair of trousers, and sues him. He loses on one count and wins on the other, and puts him into Ulysses as Private Carr, the drunken British soldier who knocks Stephen Dedalus down in the brothel episode.
stops.quote: You forget that the kingdom of heaven suffers violence: and the kingdom of heaven is like a woman.
stops.quote_source: Exiles, Act II (1918); attributed to Robert Hand, not verified against the play text in this pass
suggested_refs: The English Players' first production, The Importance of Being Earnest, Zurich, 29 April 1918
Joyce v. Carr, Zurich, 1918-1919

segments.name: Paris, the Book, and the Wake

stops.name: Via Sanita, Trieste: the city that changed
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the address; attested for the return to Trieste, October 1919 to June 1920. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: After the armistice he goes back to Trieste and finds it Italian, poorer, and emptied of the polyglot empire that made it interesting. Stanislaus is out of internment and no longer willing to be the family bank. Teaching is scarce and the Berlitz school is not what it was. In the flat on Via Sanita he finishes Circe, the longest episode, the brothel hallucination that runs to a hundred and fifty pages, and Eumaeus after it. Eight months are enough. He is looking for somewhere else and Ezra Pound is about to name it.
suggested_refs: Via Sanita, Trieste, the postwar flat of 1919-1920

stops.name: 9 rue de l'Universite, Paris: the week that lasted twenty years
stops.date_confidence: attested for July 1920; the day of arrival is approximate within the month.
stops.campa: Pound tells him to come to Paris for a week on the way to London, and borrows him an apartment. He never goes to London and he does not leave France for twenty years. He settles into the Paris literary world of cafes, patrons, small presses, and a colony of Americans with money, in a language he speaks well enough to be left alone in. Marcel Proust is living in the same city, though the two of them will not sit at the same table for two more years.
suggested_refs: 9 rue de l'Universite, Paris, the borrowed apartment of July 1920

stops.name: New York: The Little Review on trial
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1921 prosecution following serialization 1918-1920; the day given is approximate within the trial's course.
stops.campa: Margaret Anderson and Jane Heap have been running Ulysses in instalments in The Little Review since 1918. The Nausicaa episode brings the New York Society for the Suppression of Vice down on them under the Comstock Act; the court finds the magazine obscene and fines the editors. The serialization stops. No American house will touch the book after that. In Paris, where it cannot be prosecuted, the unfinished novel is being discussed by people who have not read it.
suggested_refs: The Little Review, serialization of Ulysses 1918-1920
People v. Anderson and Heap, New York, February 1921

stops.name: Shakespeare and Company, 12 rue de l'Odeon: Ulysses
stops.date_confidence: attested. The afterlife lens gave 48.8534,2.3488, about 800 m away in the 3rd arrondissement; the geography value used here agrees with OSM to within 70 m.
stops.campa: No established publisher will touch it, so Sylvia Beach, who runs a lending library and bookshop on the rue de l'Odeon and has no experience of publishing anything, brings it out herself in an edition of a thousand from a printer in Dijon. Two copies come off the Dijon train on the morning of the second of February, Joyce's fortieth birthday. That May he sits at the same supper table as Marcel Proust at the Majestic and the two of them find nothing to say; Proust is dead by November.
stops.quote: The pity is the public will demand and find a moral in my book, or worse they may take it in some more serious way.
stops.quote_source: Interview with Djuna Barnes, Vanity Fair vol. 18 no. 2, April 1922 (not March, as commonly cited); the original punctuates the break with a dash
suggested_refs: Shakespeare and Company, 12 rue de l'Odeon, Paris
Maurice Darantiere's press at Dijon, printer of the first edition

stops.name: 2 Square Robiac, Paris: Work in Progress
stops.date_confidence: attested for the tenancy, June 1925 to April 1931, his longest Paris address; the day is defaulted. Coordinate corrected from 48.8556,2.3138, about 640 m off Square Robiac.
stops.campa: In a flat off the rue de Grenelle, the longest he holds anywhere in Paris, he works on a book he will not name for sixteen years and calls only Work in Progress. Fragments appear in transition; friends and patrons read them with dismay. Harriet Shaw Weaver, who has paid for everything, asks him gently whether he might write something else. He does not. He is building a language out of forty other languages to say what a mind does between falling asleep and waking.
stops.quote: One great part of every human existence is passed in a state which cannot be rendered sensible by the use of wideawake language, cutanddry grammar and goahead plot.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Harriet Shaw Weaver, 24 November 1926; not verified against a letters edition in this pass
suggested_refs: 2 Square Robiac, off 192 rue de Grenelle, Paris
transition, serialization of Work in Progress from 1927

stops.name: Kensington Register Office, London: the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date. The coordinate is the atlas's London city pin, not the register office itself, which is in Kensington some 5 km west. The chronology lens said 'more than 27 years' after the elopement; the interval is 26 years and 9 months.
stops.campa: Twenty-six years and nine months after they left Dublin together, and with two grown children, Joyce and Nora Barnacle marry in a London register office. He gives testamentary reasons: English inheritance law, the children's standing. The registrar's clerk tips off a reporter and the news is in the papers next morning, which infuriates him. Nora, who has been called Mrs Joyce by everyone in four countries for a quarter of a century, is unimpressed by the ceremony.
suggested_refs: Kensington Register Office, London, 4 July 1931

stops.name: New York: Judge Woolsey lifts the ban
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Woolsey ruling of December 1933, affirmed by the Second Circuit in 1934.
stops.campa: Random House imports a copy deliberately so that it can be seized, and John M. Woolsey of the Southern District of New York reads the whole book and rules that it is not pornographic, that its effect is somewhat emetic but nowhere aphrodisiac, and that it may enter the United States. The Second Circuit affirms. Twelve years after the Little Review verdict the ban is over and the first authorized American edition appears. The manuscript itself ends in Philadelphia at the Rosenbach, the same building that will one day take Maurice Sendak's papers.
suggested_refs: United States v. One Book Called Ulysses (S.D.N.Y. 1933)
The Rosenbach Museum and Library, Philadelphia, holding the Ulysses manuscript

stops.name: 7 rue Edmond Valentin, Paris: Lucia
stops.date_confidence: attested for the tenancy, 1935 to April 1939; the geography lens ended it in 1938. Month and day defaulted. Coordinate corrected from 48.8608,2.3037, about 180 m off.
stops.campa: Near the Champ de Mars he finishes the last pages of the Wake while his daughter is moved between clinics. Lucia has trained as a dancer, drawn lettrines, thrown a chair at her mother, been diagnosed by a succession of doctors. Carl Jung, who once wrote that Ulysses was a worm cut lengthwise, examines her at Kusnacht in 1934 and tells the father that where he dives she falls. Joyce refuses the diagnosis for years, pays for everything, and answers her letters as though nothing were wrong.
suggested_refs: 7 rue Edmond Valentin, Paris
Carl Jung's 1934 examination of Lucia Joyce at Kusnacht

stops.name: 34 rue des Vignes, Paris: Finnegans Wake
stops.date_confidence: attested for the publication, 4 May 1939. The chronology lens said seventeen years of composition; from March 1923 it is sixteen.
stops.campa: Sixteen years after the first page, the book gets its title on the day it is published: Finnegans Wake, no apostrophe. Nora has known the title for months and kept it. Faber in London and Viking in New York issue it simultaneously in May. The reviewers are baffled and say so; his brother Stanislaus calls it drivel and his patron cannot follow it. Joyce has been told for a decade that it is unreadable and replies that it took him seventeen years to write and the reader might give it a few. He has eighteen months to live. In September the war begins.
suggested_refs: Finnegans Wake (Faber and Faber / Viking Press, 4 May 1939)
34 rue des Vignes, Paris, the last Paris address

segments.name: The Last Flight and the Zurichberg

stops.name: Saint-Gerand-le-Puy, Allier: the year of the visa
stops.date_confidence: attested for the residence December 1939 to December 1940; the day is approximate. Coordinate corrected from 46.2308,3.6667, about 12 km east of the village.
stops.campa: Fearing the bombing of Paris, the family goes to a village in the Allier where his grandson Stephen has been evacuated with his school. France falls in June. For a year Joyce writes letters: to the Swiss, who want a bond and doubt his finances and have been told he is Jewish, which he is not; to the French authorities, for permission to move Lucia out of a clinic in the occupied zone. The permission for Lucia never comes. He leaves her behind in France.
suggested_refs: Saint-Gerand-le-Puy, Allier, refuge of the Joyce family 1939-1940

stops.name: Zurich: the second arrival
stops.date_confidence: attested.
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of December the family crosses into Switzerland and reaches Zurich for the second time in a lifetime, thirty-six years after the first, when the Berlitz post turned out not to exist and a clerk sent him on to Pola. It is the same station, and Switzerland is neutral again, as it was through the other war. Nora, Giorgio and the grandson Stephen are with him. Lucia is in a clinic in occupied France, and the visa for her did not come. He has three and a half weeks left.
suggested_refs: Zurich Hauptbahnhof, 17 December 1940

stops.name: Gloriastrasse, Zurich: the perforated ulcer
stops.date_confidence: attested for the death. Coordinate corrected from 47.3775,8.5570, which sits up the Zurichberg rather than on Gloriastrasse.
stops.campa: On the eleventh of January he is operated on for a perforated duodenal ulcer that has been there, undiagnosed, for years; the pain had been put down to nerves. He rallies, then sinks. He dies before dawn on the thirteenth in the Red Cross nursing home on Gloriastrasse, fifty-eight years old, having asked whether nobody understands. Nora and Giorgio are called back too late to be there at the moment. The Irish government, invited to send a representative, does not.
suggested_refs: The Schwesternhaus vom Roten Kreuz, Gloriastrasse, Zurich

stops.name: Fluntern Cemetery, Zurich: the grave above the zoo
stops.date_confidence: attested for the burial. The two lenses gave coordinates 360 m apart; OSM and Wikipedia both give this value.
stops.campa: He is buried on the fifteenth on the slope of the Zurichberg, in a cemetery above the city and directly beside the zoo. The mourners note the lions. Lord Derwent speaks for the British legation; a tenor sings Monteverdi. Nora, asked afterwards about the Catholic rites he had refused all his life, says she could not do that to him. She lives ten more years in Zurich, mostly poor, and dies on the tenth of April 1951. She is buried at Fluntern too, in a separate grave.
suggested_refs: Friedhof Fluntern, Zurich, and the adjoining Zurich Zoo

stops.name: Martello Tower, Sandycove: the museum opens on Bloomsday
stops.date_confidence: attested.
stops.campa: The architect Michael Scott buys the gun tower at Sandycove in 1954 because it stands next to his house, and gives it away to be made a museum. It opens on the sixteenth of June 1962, with Sylvia Beach, who published the book forty years earlier in a Paris bookshop, cutting the ribbon at the door of the room the book begins in. Joyce spent about a week here in 1904 and left in the dark after a man fired a revolver over his bed. It is now the place where the day begins, every year, for people who have come from the other side of the world to walk it.
suggested_refs: The James Joyce Tower and Museum, Sandycove, opened 16 June 1962

stops.name: Fluntern Cemetery, Zurich: the honorary grave and the bronze
stops.date_confidence: attested. The afterlife lens carried the statue and reburial as tradition only; the correction pass establishes both, so the hedge is retired.
stops.campa: On Bloomsday 1966 the city of Zurich grants an honorary grave and Joyce and Nora, buried apart for fifteen years, are laid together in it. Milton Hebald's bronze is unveiled at the same hour: the man seated with his legs crossed, a book on his knee, a cigarette, the round glasses, looking down the hill. The zoo is on the other side of the wall and the lions can be heard from the grave. Ireland has never asked for the bones back, and no Irish government sent anyone to the funeral in 1941.
suggested_refs: Milton Hebald's bronze of Joyce at Fluntern, unveiled 16 June 1966
The honorary grave granted by the city of Zurich

stops.name: North Earl Street, Dublin: the statue with the stick
stops.date_confidence: attested. The afterlife lens flagged sculptor and date as an open gap; the correction closes it. Coordinate corrected from 53.3496,-6.2599, about 100 m south.
stops.campa: Marjorie Fitzgibbon's life-size bronze is unveiled on Bloomsday 1990 at the corner of North Earl Street and O'Connell Street, commissioned by the association of city-centre shopkeepers. He stands leaning on the stick, hat back, looking sideways down the street he spent thirty-six years not returning to. Dublin, which burned his book in sheets in 1912 and kept it out of the shops until the sixties, names the statue the Prick with the Stick, and means it affectionately.
suggested_refs: Marjorie Fitzgibbon's Joyce statue, North Earl Street, Dublin, unveiled 16 June 1990
